about: Recipe catalogue for the Damex Video Engine. Each recipe is one kind of motion-graphics film the engine can make from a one-line request: its triggers route the request, not_for points to the better recipe when it is the wrong one, defaults and questions fill in a thin brief, the starter prompt is the director brief to begin from, and optimise, avoid, motion and engine_gaps say what to get right. Built from the motion study of about 290 corpus records (study/*.json and notes/*.md): every record was read, and the studies measured and watched a subset (contact sheets, frame-by-frame transition windows and profile.py timings); many others were judged from prompt text or posters only, and no one listened to the audio beyond loudness. Five recipes (product-explainer, customer-story, quote-card, graphics-package, map-journey) fill gaps the corpus barely covers, so their timings are judgements, not measurements. Likes are the creator site's counts at scrape time; null means the count was not recorded, not zero, and likes partly reflect reach and timing rather than craft. References name corpus ids for study only: the prompts and videos belong to their creators, and every starter prompt here is written fresh, not copied. Engine move names are checked against engine-moves.tsv; moves in the capture-* families apply only when the film uses real screen captures. ROUTING. (1) Lower-case the brief and match triggers as phrases; the longest matching phrase wins, so "pre-launch video" beats "launch video" and "spotify canvas with lyrics" beats "spotify canvas loop". (2) If no phrase matches, match on unordered word sets: a trigger scores when all its words appear in the brief in any order. (3) Stop words never score on their own: motion graphics, animation, animated, video, film, reel, reels, promo, clip, content, something. "reel" scores only inside a longer trigger such as showreel, sizzle reel, demo reel, intro reel or portfolio reel. (4) Platform names (Instagram, Reels, TikTok, LinkedIn, YouTube Shorts) set the aspect, not the recipe: 9:16 for Reels, TikTok and Shorts, 1:1 or 4:5 for a LinkedIn, Instagram or Facebook feed. They pick social-hook-ad only when the brief asks for an ad and nothing else matches. (5) Look words (particles, 3D, glass, neon, glow, cinematic, minimal) set the design style, not the recipe; route by subject (an "AI product" is a product-launch-film). If particles are asked for, ask: "Particles read as dots, which the house style rules out; shall I use depth (3D panels, focus pulls, frosted glass) instead?" (6) Tie-breakers: a teaser or tease beats launch (product-teaser); explain, show how, how it works, under the hood or flows through beat the product type (how-it-works), unless the brief asks for an install line, benchmark or launch of a developer tool (dev-tool-film); a supplied article, blog post or newsletter goes to argument-film; a narrated explainer of the whole product goes to product-explainer; a physical product goes to product-launch-film's physical branch; updates to something that already exists go to news-recap's changelog branch. (7) Fallback: if nothing matches, ask one question, "Which is closest: launch, walkthrough, explainer, numbers, brand film or ad?" If no one can answer, use product-launch-film when the brief names a product or feature, and brand-spot when it names only the brand. ENERGY. Every starter has an Energy line with calm, confident and hype pacing; it sets shot length, easing and still time and overrides any other pacing words in that starter, but it does not change the recipe's number of beats unless it says so. The brief's words set {energy}: calm, quiet, gentle, relaxing and soothing mean calm; slick, premium, Apple-like, cinematic and elegant mean confident, centred, one accent and longer shots (in brand-spot they take the calm-or-premium branch); punchy, hype, energetic, bold, launch day and drop mean hype. Otherwise use the recipe's default. The audience can override a tone word when it plainly does not fit (a parenting app asked for hype and was better calm, pm:francoxavier33-d2dfd2). Targets per energy, in profile.py units: typical motion hype 4.4 to 6.5, confident 1.2 to 1.7, calm 0.5 to 0.9 (illustrated character stories run higher); still time under 10% for hype and confident, 13 to 15% for calm. PLACEHOLDERS. {length}, {aspect}, {energy} and {fps} come from defaults unless the brief says otherwise. {bpm} is 120, or 128 when the energy is hype. {cta} is the product's web address. {launch_date} is "coming soon". {audience} is the brand's customers. {install_line} is the first install command in the README. {device} is desktop unless an app store, iOS, Android or a phone is named. {speaker} is the person in the clip or the person quoted. {artist} is {brand} for a jingle; {song} must be supplied. {name} and {role} come from the portfolio. Required, with no default: {data_source} (stat-story), {source} (timeline-history, news-recap, portfolio-reel, customer-story, map-journey) and {customer} (customer-story); if one is not supplied, ask for it and do not build. RENDER. Every starter ends with the render line: 1920x1080, 1080x1920, 1080x1080 or 1080x1350 (4:5, for feeds), the recipe's fps, subframe motion blur from 8 or more subframes, and the length within 0.1 s. Every starter asks for a checkpoint (beat list with times and stills) before the full render. House rules from knowledge/craft/13-design-styles.md still apply, including its ban on dots, mesh blobs, glitch and RGB split, which many popular references use; where a recipe needs a carried object it uses the brand's mark, a square or a full stop instead of a dot. Merged categories: phone app promos and physical-product showcases sit in product-launch-film (the former app-promo recipe was merged into it); app update reels and changelogs sit in news-recap; 3D and WebGL pieces are spread across ambient-scene-loop, beat-visualiser and how-it-works; event promos, event recaps, greetings and hiring posts sit in occasion-post; mascot-led story promos sit in illustrated-short; studio credential reels sit in motion-showreel; narrated essays sit in argument-film; audiograms and podcast trailers sit in kinetic-type. Experiments and remakes, and game or interactive captures, have no recipe, because asking for a game or a remake does not produce a directed film.

families.name: Product

families.name: Data

families.name: Abstract

recipes.name: Product launch film and app promo
recipes.summary: A 15 to 30 second launch film that states one promise at a time and proves each one with the real product on screen, joined by one continuous camera; for a phone app it becomes a vertical promo with the phone held in place and its screen changing, and for a physical product each promise is a detail of the object.
triggers: hero video for the landing page
not_for: a 6 to 15 second paid social ad built on one hook: social-hook-ad
a pre-launch tease with one hero gesture and no feature list: product-teaser
one user flow shown step by step with the cursor: feature-walkthrough
a film whose spine is a price or a sale: price-offer-film
a developer tool, API or CLI: dev-tool-film
showing step by step how to use one feature: feature-walkthrough
anything asking for a teaser or tease, even if it says launch: product-teaser
updates or a changelog for an app or product that already exists: news-recap
a 60 to 90 s narrated film about what the product does: product-explainer

structure.what: The problem or the promise as one readable line by 1.0 s; the product's first real moment on screen by 2.0 s.

structure.share: about 55% (four beats of 2.5 to 3 s; on a phone, five chapters of 2 to 2.5 s)
structure.what: Each beat: a short headline alone on the page, then the real interface doing exactly that within about a second, driven by a cursor. Each scene is built from an object in the one before.
One surprise taken from the product: a toggle that floods the film into a second colour, a button that becomes the next scene, a tile pushed through until its colour is the next page.
Mark, name and address or button; 1 to 1.75 s of true stillness at the very end.

recipes.starter_prompt: Make a {length} launch film for {product} by {brand}, in {aspect}. The film has one job: to make the viewer believe {message}. Before designing anything, read the product's site, code or design files and list three or four promises it really keeps, each with a real screen, number or result that proves it. Never invent figures. Put a readable line on screen by the first second and the product by the second. Give each promise one beat of about 2.5 to 3 seconds: a short headline alone on the page, then the real interface doing that thing within about a second, moved by a large cursor. Use one light page, one typeface, one accent colour for the single word that matters, and headlines at least 6% of frame height. Treat it as one continuous camera. Every new scene is made from something already on screen: a button becomes a card, a tile's colour becomes the next page. Keep every pause under a second until the end card. No crossfades, no fades through black, no text cards on black between shots. Plan one surprise at the turn of the story, such as a control whose colour floods the frame. Ease out on every arrival and keep overshoot under 2%. Device: {device}. If phone, lead with 9:16: the headline sits in the top third with one word marked by a highlighter stroke, the phone stays fixed in the lower two thirds and its screen changes in place rather than cutting, the icon and name are on screen by 1.5 seconds, and five chapters of 2 to 2.5 seconds each get their own tint or interaction so the rhythm never feels even. If the product is physical, each promise is a macro detail or a turntable angle of the object, lit as a packshot, with no cursor and no interface. End on the mark, the name and {cta}, still for about a second and a half. Leave out particle bursts, glows, confetti, logo walls, stat rows, stock lifestyle footage and generic gradient blobs. Energy: {energy}; it sets the pacing inside the beats above, not their number. If calm: one slow move every 3 to 4 s, long ease-in-out settles with no overshoot, still time 13 to 15%, typical motion about 0.5 to 0.9. If confident: a new move or picture every 1.5 to 2.5 s, ease-out arrivals with overshoot under 2%, still time under 10%, typical motion about 1.2 to 1.7. If hype: a cut or a new word every 0.5 to 1 s on the beat, entries that smear in and settle in about 5 frames, still time under 10%, typical motion about 4.4 to 6.5. Show me the beat list and four stills before rendering the whole film. Render at 1920x1080 (16:9), 1080x1920 (9:16), 1080x1080 (1:1) or 1080x1350 (4:5), {fps} fps, with subframe motion blur from 8 or more subframes, delivered within 0.1 s of {length}.
questions: What one thing should a viewer believe after watching? [the main promise on the product's home page]
Can I read the site, repo or design files for real screens and numbers? [yes, the public site]

Is it a phone app, a web or desktop product, or a physical object? [read it from the brief: an app store, iOS, Android or phone means phone]
Particles read as dots, which the house style rules out; shall I use depth (3D panels, focus pulls, frosted glass) instead? [ask only when the brief asks for particles; default yes]

recipes.name: Teaser and announcement sting
recipes.summary: A 10 to 20 second precise tease built on one hero gesture taken from the product, ending on the name and a date or 'coming soon'.
not_for: a full launch with three or four promises: product-launch-film
just the logo animating: logo-reveal
a fast paid ad with a hook and a call to action: social-hook-ad
a single UI element morphing through many states: ui-morph-loop

structure.what: One sentence builds word by word and poses the problem or question; the product name may appear by 1 s.
The one move that belongs to the product (the notch that grows into a panel, a menu-bar prompt that springs out, a lid that closes), staged with a slow camera and focus pulls.
One result or card rising over the blurred product; no feature list.
Name with 'coming soon' or the date; hold about 1.5 s or end on a still-moving shrink.

recipes.starter_prompt: Make a {length} teaser for {product} by {brand}, in {aspect}. It should leave the viewer wanting to know more about {message}, without listing features. Find the one gesture that belongs to this product and nothing else, such as a panel growing out of a menu bar, a lid closing or a field filling itself, and build the film around it. If the hero is a dashboard: panels arrive one at a time in reading order, charts draw to real or supplied sample data, numbers roll to rest, and one camera push lands on the key figure. Open with one sentence that builds word by word and is readable in the first second. Energy {energy}. Calm: one slow camera, moves of 1.5 to 3 s that never reverse, still time 13 to 15%. Confident: camera moves of about 1 to 1.5 s and a cut every 2 s or so, still time under 10%. Hype: cuts two frames before the beat every 0.5 to 1 s, word slams, a countdown to {launch_date}, still time under 10%. Each shot is already in motion when it appears and speeds away or smears out when it goes, so nothing sits on a frozen frame. Entrances start fast and settle long. Keep it to the brand's light page, one typeface, real interface recreated faithfully, soft depth from focus and frosted panels, and one accent. Close on the name with 'coming soon' or {launch_date}, held for about a second and a half. Do not use crossfades, white flashes, glows on interface text, particle bursts or stock launch rings around an icon. Before the full render, show me four stills: the opening line, the hero gesture mid-move, the proof and the end card. Render at 1920x1080 (16:9), 1080x1920 (9:16), 1080x1080 (1:1) or 1080x1350 (4:5), {fps} fps, with subframe motion blur from 8 or more subframes, delivered within 0.1 s of {length}.
questions: What is the one gesture or moment that belongs only to this product? [the main control in its interface]
Is there a launch date to show? [no: 'coming soon']
Should it have sound? [a soft track at about 100 BPM, cuts two frames before the beat]
Is there real or sample data for a dashboard hero? [use the product's own demo data; never invent figures presented as real]
optimise: A readable sentence in the first second (pm:jake11moran-f60e35, pm:notdwd-7de38a).
When calm: camera moves of 1.5 to 3 s on a gentle ease-in-out; one continuous camera (pm:jake11moran-f60e35). When hype: cuts every 0.5 to 1 s, two frames before the beat.
Entries start fast and settle long: use the arrive easing token (cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)); keep moving at least 85% of the time (pm:notdwd-7de38a is 12% still).
Hard cuts, if any, land two frames before the beat (pm:notdwd-7de38a: within one frame of the plan).
Moving for at least 85% of the running time; no empty frames.
One hero gesture given at least half the film.
No more than one proof card; no feature list.
Contrast stays readable on dark: no grey type on charcoal (pm:robj3d3-b18fad).
End hold 1 to 1.75 s, or end on a moving shrink.
Length 10 to 20 s.
avoid: Dark, low-contrast frames where nothing is legible for seconds (pm:robj3d3-b18fad).
A glowing app icon in concentric rings on dark, the stock launch opener (pm:ezshine-c90d73 poster).
Listing all features.
Corner timecodes and frame labels.
A long still end card.
Rotating lists too fast to read unless the speed is the joke (pm:jake11moran-f60e35).

recipes.name: Feature walkthrough
recipes.summary: A 20 to 40 second film that follows one user flow through the real interface, step by step, so the viewer sees exactly how the product does its job.
triggers: show the workflow in the product
not_for: a launch that sells three or four promises: product-launch-film
one element morphing through states as a loop: ui-morph-loop
explaining an idea or mechanism rather than a product flow: how-it-works
a phone-first app promo or app store video: product-launch-film
a recipe or physical how-to: step-by-step
how data or money moves through a back-end system: how-it-works
a narrated film about what the whole product does: product-explainer

structure.what: One line naming what the user wants done; the problem visible by 2.5 s.

structure.share: about 70% (four or five steps of about 4 s)
structure.what: One object carried through every step (one post, one document, one request). Cursor types, clicks and approves; camera zooms so each step fills the frame. A step tracker or tab bar shows where we are.
The finished outcome shown large, with one true number if there is one.
Mark, name and where to try it.

recipes.starter_prompt: Make a {length} walkthrough of {product} by {brand}, in {aspect}, showing how a user gets {message} done. Read the product or its site first and write the flow as four or five steps in the user's words. Pick one thing (a post, a file, a request) and carry that same thing through every step, so the viewer follows one story rather than a list. Rebuild the real interface as components rather than pasting screenshots, and keep it large: the camera eases in before each action so the part being used fills 55 to 75% of the frame width, holds through the action and eases out. A large cursor causes every change: typing at a human rhythm, clicks with a small press, drags that the interface follows. Show progress with the product's own device, such as a step bar or tab bar. Give each step about four seconds in a 30 s film (about three in a 20 s cut), change something every second, and never repeat the same layout or the same typing beat more than twice. Product words at least 4% of frame height, other text at least 2.6%. One light page, one typeface, one accent. No narration slides, no fades through black, no confetti. End on the finished result, then the name and {cta} held for about a second and a half. Energy: {energy}; it sets the pacing inside the beats above, not their number. If calm: one slow move every 3 to 4 s, long ease-in-out settles with no overshoot, still time 13 to 15%, typical motion about 0.5 to 0.9. If confident: a new move or picture every 1.5 to 2.5 s, ease-out arrivals with overshoot under 2%, still time under 10%, typical motion about 1.2 to 1.7. If hype: a cut or a new word every 0.5 to 1 s on the beat, entries that smear in and settle in about 5 frames, still time under 10%, typical motion about 4.4 to 6.5. Show me the step list and a still of each step first. Render at 1920x1080 (16:9), 1080x1920 (9:16), 1080x1080 (1:1) or 1080x1350 (4:5), {fps} fps, with subframe motion blur from 8 or more subframes, delivered within 0.1 s of {length}.
questions: Which single flow should the viewer see? [the one on the product's home page]
Is there a voice-over? [no: short on-screen lines]
Can I use real screens or recordings? [rebuild from the live site]
optimise: The job is readable by 1 s and the problem on screen by 2.5 s.
Four or five steps of about 4 s in a 30 s film (about 3 s in a 20 s cut); never 7 s per step (pm:charlesmendez-73b6e4 ran 57 s).
One carried object through every step (pm:miskinho-443898).

The subject fills 55 to 75% of the frame width (05-ui-choreography.md); product words at least 4% and other text at least 2.6% of frame height (08-directors-checks.md); pm:demonugc-4c5753 at about a tenth of the width read as empty.
Still time under 15% (strong films 0 to 16%; weak ones 27 to 68%).
The cursor is the cause of every change.
A progress device that belongs to the product (pm:kmasiff-cc72cb tab bar, pm:ajith-io-c52e09 three-segment bar).
No layout used more than twice in a row.
Length stated and enforced: 20 to 40 s; open briefs ran 23 to 76 s.
End card 1 to 1.75 s still.

Long typing beats repeated (pm:lester-tyy-f897f7, 76 s).

recipes.summary: A 20 to 60 second drawn or modelled story with a character, a clear want and an ending, often in one fixed set, which can promote a product quietly at the end.

a product promo with a mascot host: product-launch-film

structure.what: One fixed set or frame; the character and what they want in the first few seconds.
The obstacle; the world changes around the character (time of day, weather, objects arriving).

recipes.starter_prompt: Make a {length} animated short in {aspect} for {brand}. Write a small story first: one character, what they want, what stands in the way and how it ends, about {message}. If the product appears, let it come from the story's own world and only near the end. Keep the frame mostly fixed, such as one set, one window or one stage, and let the world change inside it: light moving from day to night, weather arriving, objects coming and going. Hide scene changes behind things that would really pass, such as a curtain, a passing vehicle or a tunnel. Give the character life: blinks, breathing, expression changes on each event, squash and stretch on hops. Hold no shot longer than about six seconds without something meaningful moving.
